paras: The killing of Philip Johnson took place at Campti, in Natchitoches Parish, Louisiana, around January 12, 1903, when two deputy sheriffs shot to death a leader of a Black religious group, the Church of God, as they tried to arrest him. Johnson had been ordered out of Campti by a committee of citizens and was killed after he returned. Two weeks later the parish's district judge cited deaths at Campti in a widely reprinted grand jury charge against mob violence.

Johnson was described as 'another leader' of the Church of God, organized by a man the dispatch called 'the negro prophet, Smith.' According to the same dispatch, Smith had founded the church in Houston, Texas, was driven from that town, and was then ordered out of Shreveport by the police along with his followers. The group moved to Bossier Parish, where 'trouble ensued,' ending in the murder of the planter John Gray Foster and the lynching of Smith and another leader of the church.

Johnson then moved to Campti, where a committee of citizens ordered him to leave, and he left. He came back on about January 12 and was shot to death by two deputy sheriffs who tried to arrest him. The dispatch gave no charge for the arrest, no names for the deputies, and no account of the shooting beyond its outcome.

On January 28 the district judge of Natchitoches Parish charged the grand jury to indict or impeach justices of the peace and other officials who had failed to suppress mob violence. He cited the lynching of a Black man at Robeline, 'two shot to death at Campti' and two others beaten at Clarence, without naming the victims. 'To say that the courts and the laws are inadequate to the punishment of the negro when he deserves punishment, and to his protection when he is entitled to protection,' he said, 'is to confess that our race is incapable of administering the government.'
The Sun's correspondent reported that indictments were expected after the charge. No report of an inquest, indictment or trial for Johnson's death was found in the coverage.

The killing reached print through a New Orleans dispatch dated January 13, which the New York Sun ran on its front page under the headline 'Negro Church Leader Shot. Was Ordered Out of Town and Came Back Killed on Sight.' The Democratic Advocate of Westminster, Maryland, reprinted the dispatch word for word on January 17. Both versions reported the deputies' action without comment and framed Johnson through the Bossier Parish violence attributed to Smith's church.

The judge's charge drew far wider notice than the killing itself. The Sun carried it on January 29 under 'Must Protect Negroes,' and the Vermont Watchman reprinted that story on February 5. The New Haven Journal and Courier called it 'a pretty good point' and wrote that the white race 'ought to govern by law instead of lawlessness,' while the Richmond Times Dispatch, under 'A Brave and Sensible Judge,' declared, 'Lucky the community that has a wise and courageous judge like that.'

No Black-press report of Johnson's killing was found. The Cleveland Gazette printed the judge's words on February 14 under the heading 'Confession,' without his list of incidents, followed by a Youngstown (Ohio) Telegram comment that 'mob attacks on colored persons' showed 'the so-called white government' to be lacking in 'some essentials of civilization.'

The dispatch names only Johnson as killed, while the judge's charge speaks of two shot to death at Campti, so the coverage leaves open whether a second person died there. The two sources also frame the deaths differently: the dispatch attributes Johnson's death to deputies making an arrest, while the judge listed the Campti killings among the mob violence local officials had failed to stop.

reader.title: Killing of Philip Johnson
bases: The only account of the shooting says two deputy sheriffs killed Johnson while trying to arrest him after he returned to a town a citizens' committee had ordered him to leave (A1); the district judge later listed the Campti deaths among mob violence (A3).

Johnson was killed, but the only report names two deputy sheriffs attempting an arrest, not a group of three or more acting outside the law (A1). The judge's charge counting 'two shot to death at Campti' among mob violence (A3) leaves room for doubt that the coverage does not resolve.
Johnson's killing rests on one New Orleans dispatch (A1, reprinted in A2); the judge's charge independently refers to two shot to death at Campti but names no one and gives no details (A3).

accounts.label: New Orleans wire dispatch
accounts.gist: Johnson was ordered away from Campti by a committee of citizens, left, returned, and was shot to death by two deputy sheriffs who tried to arrest him.

accounts.label: District judge's grand jury charge
accounts.gist: The judge counted 'two shot to death at Campti' among acts of mob violence that local officials had failed to suppress and called for indictments.

framing.detail: The Sun headlined the dispatch 'Negro Church Leader Shot. Was Ordered Out of Town and Came Back Killed on Sight' and gave the officers' action without comment.
Northern and Southern editorials quoted the judge's charge and praised it, the New Haven paper saying the white race 'ought to govern by law instead of lawlessness'.
The Cleveland Gazette ran the judge's words under 'Confession.' with a Youngstown Telegram comment calling mob attacks proof of failed white government; it did not name Campti or Johnson.

conflicts.note: The dispatch does not say Johnson was the only one killed; the judge's charge names no victims, so a second death at Campti, or a different incident, cannot be settled from the coverage.
